title: A CNN-based mapping approach for aeolian dunes in Arctic Sweden
summary: Aeolian dunes provide valuable evidence of past wind regimes and environmental change but mapping them reliably over large areas remains challenging. Manual delineation of dune boundaries is time-consuming and difficult to apply consistently. Automated approaches also struggle where vegetation partly obscures dune morphology and where sand-rich fluvial surfaces, such as riverbanks and terraces, exhibit spectral responses similar to those of stabilized dunes. In this study, dune mapping is treated as a pixel-wise binary segmentation task that separates dune-covered areas, including adjoining or overlapping dunes, from the surrounding background. We present ArcticSandNet, a multimodal segmentation network based on the U-Net architecture. Optical imagery and terrain variables derived from a digital elevation model (DEM), including elevation, slope, and curvature, are processed by two separate encoders. Their features are combined at each encoder level through feature concatenation. In the decoder, an attention-based module fuses encoder skips features with upsampled decoder features, helping the network retain dune-related spatial information while suppressing responses from heterogeneous background surfaces. The model was trained and evaluated across 15 sites in northern Sweden using spatial five-fold cross-validation. A further site was excluded from all model training, validation, and selection procedures and retained solely for independent testing. In cross-validation, ArcticSandNet achieved a two-class mean intersection over union (mIoU) of 78.15% ± 5.34% and a two-class mean F1 score (mF1) of 85.97% ± 4.78%. For the dune class, it achieved an F1 score of 72.61% ± 8.46% and an IoU of 57.63% ± 9.59%, outperforming U-Net, SegNet, and Attention U-Net trained under the same settings. On the independent test site, ArcticSandNet achieved a dune-class recall of 60.52%, an F1 score of 67.16%, and an IoU of 50.55%, also outperforming the three benchmark networks in dune-class F1 and IoU. The resulting maps of dune-covered areas provide a consistent spatial basis for regional analyses of dune-field characteristics, morphology, and landscape stability.

title: Dust aerosol properties and radiative effects over the global oceans from synergistic spaceborne observations and modeling
summary: The microphysical and radiative properties of mineral dust aerosols, a major species of atmospheric aerosols, are fundamental to quantifying broad dust aerosol impacts. At present, substantial uncertainties remain in estimating dust microphysical properties and radiative effects on a global scale, stemming from source-dependent mineralogical variability that leads to substantial varaiations in dust optical and microphysical properties, as well as inconsistencies in the physical assumptions adopted in spaceborne retrievals and radiative transfer simulations. This study develops a physically consistent approach for retrieving dust aerosol properties over the global oceans and to quantify the associated radiative effects through the synergistic use of collocated observations made by the Cloud-Aerosol Lidar with Orthogonal Polarization (CALIOP) and the Infrared Imaging Radiometer (IIR) aboard the Cloud-Aerosol Lidar and Infrared Pathfinder Satellite Observations (CALIPSO) platform. The new retrieval algorithm uses the TAMUdust2020 dust single-scattering property database, which represents dust in terms of an ensemble of randomly distorted hexahedral particles, and incorporates a region- and mineralogy-dependent refractive index dataset, and avoids an empirical lidar-ratio assumption. The retrieved dust properties are incorporated into a dust optical property parameterization for the Rapid Radiative Transfer Model for Global Climate Models (RRTMG), ensuring that a consistent representation of dust optical and microphysical properties is used for both the retrieval implementation and downstream radiative transfer calculations. To quantify the influence of regional mineralogical variability and longwave scattering on the simulated radiative effects, this study also presents the global and seasonal distributions of dust aerosol optical thickness, effective particle radius, vertical structure, and associated radiative effects over the global oceans. The present findings show that dust exerts shortwave (SW) cooling and longwave (LW) warming over the global oceans, with area-weighted annual mean SW/LW effects of −1.358/+0.329 W m −2 at the surface and − 0.796/+0.029 W m −2 at the top of the atmosphere, respectively.

title: Assessing the spatio-temporal cumulative drought effects on two Mediterranean forest types in Central Chile
summary: Droughts are long-lasting events that can drive persistent functional changes in ecosystems, particularly in drought-prone areas like Mediterranean forests. We integrated a phenology-based anomaly method, combining kernel density estimation (KDE) with cumulative sums (CUSUMs) to assess long-term drought impacts on two Mediterranean forest types in Central Chile. Using MODIS Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI), the Moisture Stress Index (MSI), and Evapotranspiration (ET) from 2000 to 2024, we quantified cumulative deviations in canopy productivity, moisture conditions, and energy exchange. Our framework revealed persistent negative functional trajectories preceding the well-documented 2010–present megadrought. Spatially explicit metrics identified coherent degradation hotspots in northern sclerophyllous and southern deciduous forests, where canopy greenness, moisture, and evapotranspiration declined synchronously. Seasonal models indicated a post-2010 strengthening of soil–water controls over forest functioning, with soil moisture and water storage variables becoming influential predictors. The convergence of cumulative negative EVI, MSI, and ET signals highlights widespread and sustained functional weakening under prolonged drought conditions. Our results demonstrate that integrating KDE-derived anomalies with cumulative deviation tracking provides a sensitive and transferable framework to detect early and persistent vegetation stress in water-limited ecosystems.

title: Prior-Informed Spatially Adaptive Network (PISA-Net) for multi-parameter water quality retrieval in Poyang Lake using Sentinel-2 imagery
summary: Accurate retrieval of water-quality parameters from remote-sensing imagery is essential for monitoring large inland lakes, yet pronounced spatial heterogeneity and limited transferability across varying environmental conditions remain major challenges. This study proposes a Prior-Informed Spatially Adaptive Network (PISA-Net) for multi-parameter water-quality retrieval from Sentinel-2 imagery in Poyang Lake. PISA-Net integrates a CNN branch for nonlinear spectral–spatial feature learning with a knowledge-guided branch based on empirical optical descriptors and coordinate-derived geographic priors. A geographic soft-assignment mechanism constructs the spatial prior vector, which conditions CNN features through Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), while a stop gradient consistency loss (SG-CL) promotes agreement between the two prediction pathways with controlled gradient propagation. Chl-a, TP, and CODMn were modeled independently and evaluated using 5-fold spatial-block cross-validation against six representative empirical, statistical, machine-learning, and deep-learning baselines. PISA-Net achieved R 2 values of 0.6113, 0.5112, and 0.5054 for Chl-a, TP, and CODMn, respectively, consistently outperforming the strongest baseline, 2D-CNN, while reducing RMSE by approximately 29.6%, 21.4%, and 19.0%. An additional April 2018 cross-season experiment revealed substantial degradation under direct zero-shot transfer, whereas few-shot adaptation markedly reduced prediction errors, indicating useful cross-season adaptability after limited local calibration. Overall, PISA-Net provides a prior-informed spectral–spatial framework for water-quality retrieval under spatially heterogeneous conditions, while broader multi-season validation remains necessary to establish comprehensive seasonal generalizability.

title: Developing broadband spectral index for estimating crop canopy water content
summary: Crop canopy water content (CWC) is an important indicator for monitoring crop growth and drought stress. However, broadband spectral indices often exhibit nonlinear and saturated responses to CWC because NIR structural scattering and SWIR water-absorption responses progressively approach saturation as leaf area index (LAI) and equivalent water thickness (EWT) increase. Because CWC is jointly determined by LAI and EWT, this study developed a physically based broadband spectral index, the Differential Ratio Water Index (DRWI), using Sentinel-2 multispectral instrument bands to couple canopy structural information from the near-infrared and red-edge regions with water-sensitive shortwave-infrared responses. PROSAIL-based global sensitivity analysis showed that DRWI had substantial and relatively balanced sensitivity to both LAI and EWT. On the independent simulated holdout dataset, DRWI showed a strong association with CWC (R 2 = 0.85) and reduced response compression compared with conventional indices. Independent validation using field-measured corn data showed that DRWI generally achieved the best numerical performance among the evaluated indices, although its advantage varied among growth stages. On the multi-crop SPARC03 dataset, DRWI achieved an R 2 of 0.58 and an rRMSE of 33.64 %, compared with an R 2 of 0.54 for LSWI. DRWI provides a physically interpretable and computationally simple approach for regional CWC estimation using widely available Sentinel-2 observations. Its predictive performance remained limited at the corn heading stage, and further evaluation across additional crop types, regions, and complete growth cycles is needed.

title: Development and validation of a red-edge-based index for improving satellite detection of algal blooms in inland waters
summary: The increasing frequency of freshwater algal blooms threatens aquatic ecosystems globally. While remote sensing algorithms are widely used for bloom detection, conventional methods frequently exhibit degraded performance under optically complex conditions (e.g., sunglint, thin clouds, and high turbidity) and lack sensitivity to sparse blooms. To address these limitations, this study introduces the Red-Edge Floating Algae Index (RFAI). Structured as a baseline-height model, the RFAI mathematically isolates the scattering-induced spectral curvature of algal blooms using three critical Sentinel-2 Multispectral Instrument (MSI) bands: the green reflectance peak (∼560 nm), the red absorption trough (∼665 nm), and the red-edge reflectance peak (∼704 nm). This formulation effectively decouples genuine target signals from confounding background noise. Comparative validation against 17 widely used indices across a diverse set of inland lakes demonstrated the statistically significant overall effectiveness of the RFAI ( p < 0.0001), yielding precision and F1-score improvements of up to 42.8 % and 26.6 %, respectively, under locally optimized parameterizations. Crucially, the RFAI demonstrates robust comprehensive stability across highly variable, optically challenging conditions, effectively mitigating the severe performance fluctuations often observed in individual conventional indices. Supported by a novel optical-type-stratified thresholding strategy, the RFAI establishes a scalable and versatile framework for operational bloom monitoring using compatible red-edge satellite systems, enabling the generation of reliable observational records essential for the sustainable management of aquatic ecosystems.

title: A Metro-InSAR Risk Index for corridor-scale displacement risk diagnosis of urban rail infrastructure
summary: Time-series Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) provides dense displacement observations along urban rail corridors, yet converting point-based measurements into corridor-scale diagnostic information remains challenging. This study proposes the Metro-InSAR Risk Index (MIRI), a diagnostic index designed to convert multi-dimensional InSAR-derived displacement characteristics into displacement-related diagnostic levels for urban metro corridors. MIRI integrates displacement rate, cumulative displacement, local displacement heterogeneity, height-related variability, and temporal residual variability, thereby extending conventional velocity-based interpretation toward corridor-scale displacement-risk diagnosis. The framework was applied to the Kunming Metro Network using 198 descending Sentinel-1 images acquired from March 2018 to December 2024. The time-series InSAR results show that the network was generally stable, with line-of-sight (LOS) displacement rates mainly ranging from −6 to 3 mm/yr and 97.21% of coherent scatterers falling within the stable interval of −3 to 3 mm/yr. Localized displacement anomalies were mainly observed near line intersections, curved sections, construction-affected areas, and the Dianchi Lake shoreline. Based on MIRI, 78%, 17%, 4%, and 1% of valid points were classified as Levels D, C, B, and A, respectively, indicating a distribution dominated by lower diagnostic levels, with spatially confined Level-B and Level-A anomalies particularly along Lines 4 and 5 and in lakeside soft-ground areas. Multi-source contextual variables and XGBoost-SHAP analysis were further used to interpret the environmental, anthropogenic, operational, and displacement-gradient information associated with the MIRI-based diagnostic patterns. The results indicate that the spatial variation in MIRI is mainly associated with terrain-related conditions, corridor-scale displacement variation, metro operation, and urban development intensity. By deriving diagnostic levels directly from PSI-based displacement indicators, MIRI provides an InSAR-based screening tool for prioritizing displacement-related anomalies and supporting maintenance of urban rail transit systems.

title: Deep learning detection of submesoscale eddies from MODIS SST in the South China Sea
summary: Submesoscale eddies play crucial roles in oceanic energy cascades and material transport; however, their detection faces substantial challenges owing to inadequate spatial resolution in traditional satellite altimetric measurements. This research introduces Sub-Eddy-Net, an innovative deep learning approach utilizing an enhanced YOLOv8-SGAM architecture for identifying submesoscale eddy features within MODIS-derived sea surface temperature (SST) imagery across the South China Sea region. By exploiting SST data's advantageous temporal coverage and observational continuity relative to altimetric sensors, synthetic aperture radar, and ocean color products, the developed algorithm demonstrates detection precision of 0.968, successfully identifying 20,443 submesoscale eddies throughout 2015–2024. Results indicate cyclonic eddy prevalence exceeds anticyclonic occurrences, exhibiting average radii of 13.1 km and 13.7 km respectively. Eddy distributions primarily cluster within coastal waters and Luzon Strait vicinity, displaying pronounced seasonal patterns. Comparison with Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) observations shows 64.3% matched features, 27.1% positional offsets, and 8.6% detected only in SST. Within the same eddies, coherent chlorophyll-a (Chla) signatures were present in a smaller fraction, indicating that SST is the more robust tracer for systematic detection. This Sub-Eddy-Net methodology offers a scalable approach for examining submesoscale oceanic phenomena, providing a decadal inventory for further study of their roles in ocean circulation and vertical exchange.

title: Reconstructing multi-temporal Glacier area changes to improve mass balance estimates in the Southeastern Tibetan Plateau (2000–2025)
summary: The southeastern Tibetan Plateau (SETP), a critical component of the “Asian Water Tower”, hosts a large concentration of maritime temperate glaciers that are highly sensitive to climate change. However, persistent cloud cover, seasonal snow, and supraglacial debris complicate consistent long-term glacier mapping, while the use of static glacier boundaries may introduce temporal mismatches in altimetry-based glacier mass-change estimates. In this study, we developed a multi-source data-fusion framework on Google Earth Engine (GEE) to reconstruct glacier-area changes in the SETP from 2000 to 2025 at five-year intervals and 30 m spatial resolution. Random Forest classifiers were used to integrate Landsat and Sentinel-2 optical imagery, Sentinel-1 synthetic-aperture-radar data, and NASADEM-derived topographic information, supporting glacier delineation under complex surface and atmospheric conditions. The reconstructed glacier area decreased from 8,083 ± 664 km2 in 2000 to 6,228 ± 572 km2 in 2025, corresponding to a cumulative loss of 22.9 ± 3.6% and a mean loss rate of 80.51 ± 10.51 km2 yr−1. The mean area-loss rates were 51.31 ± 6.51 km2 yr−1 during 2000–2010 and 92.99 ± 15.55 km2 yr−1 during 2010–2025, indicating a higher average loss rate in the later period. By combining satellite-altimetry-derived elevation changes from ICESat, CryoSat-2, and ICESat-2 with the reconstructed time-varying glacier areas, we estimated a mean glacier mass-change rate of −6.51 ± 1.22 Gt yr−1 during 2003–2022. Compared with using a fixed 2003 glacier area, the time-varying-area calculation reduced the estimated mass-loss magnitude by 0.63 Gt yr−1, equivalent to 8.8% of the fixed-area estimate. These results indicate that incorporating time-varying glacier areas can reduce temporal mismatch in altimetry-based mass-change estimation and improve the temporal consistency of regional glacier mass-change assessments.

title: Transforming Leaf-Off LiDAR to leaf-on canopy height models using deep learning
summary: Accurate tree canopy metrics are essential for a wide range of ecological, environmental, and climate studies. Recent advances in airborne LiDAR sensing have greatly expanded access to high-resolution three-dimensional observations of tree canopy structure. However, many widely available airborne LiDAR datasets are acquired under leaf-off conditions to support terrain mapping, and our analysis across ecologically diverse sites shows that canopy height models (CHMs) derived from these data exhibit substantial, recurring discrepancies in canopy height and extent, with an overall tendency to underrepresent canopy structure relative to leaf-on conditions. These discrepancies limit the direct use of leaf-off CHMs in applications requiring canopy information representative of leaf-on conditions. To address this limitation, we introduce a deep learning framework for reconstructing leaf-on CHMs from existing leaf-off LiDAR-derived CHMs. To our knowledge, this is the first study to formulate the direct reconstruction of leaf-on CHMs from existing leaf-off LiDAR-derived CHMs as a supervised image-to-image learning task. The framework provides two complementary models: a Pix2Pix model that uses the leaf-off CHM alone and a U-Net model that additionally incorporates multispectral imagery. Our proposed models achieve robust canopy-height accuracy across four spatially independent test sites (R²: 0.85–0.92; Mean Absolute Error: 1.3–1.6 metres), substantially reducing the discrepancies observed in the leaf-off source CHMs. They also provide sharper delineation of canopy details and higher accuracy than recent optical-imagery-based approaches. To facilitate broader use, we developed an open-access web application that deploys the pre-trained models and supports on-demand leaf-on CHM generation for user-selected areas across the U.S. where suitable leaf-off LiDAR inputs are available. Overall, the framework provides a practical means to bridge the seasonal data gap in LiDAR acquisition and improve access to reliable canopy metrics representative of leaf-on conditions.

title: Second-dimension-enhanced spatial context-aware modeling for spatial prediction
summary: Spatial prediction is a fundamental task in geographic information science and environmental resource assessment. However, under complex terrain and heterogeneous covariates, models relying only on point-scale attributes or a single global relationship often have difficulty representing spatial context and regional heterogeneity. This study proposes a second-dimension-enhanced spatial context-aware modeling framework (SDA-SCA) that integrates first-dimension covariates, neighborhood-based second-dimension features, covariate screening, spatially constrained stratification, and local model training. Using two independently constructed annual spatial-prediction cases based on surface solar radiation observations from 670 stations in China in 2022 and 2023, five modeling schemes—Ordinary Kriging, Geographically Weighted Random Forest (GWRF), first-dimension attribute modeling (FDA), second-dimension augmented modeling (SDA), and SDA-SCA—were evaluated under spatial cross-validation. SDA-SCA showed a consistent predictive advantage across the two independent annual cases and the three evaluated model families. Relative to FDA, SDA-SCA increased R2 by 0.11–0.16 in 2022 and 0.17–0.21 in 2023, while reducing RMSE by 12.4%–17.7% and 24.3%–33.7%, and MAE by 22.8%–35.5% and 31.5%–50.4%, respectively. Stage-wise ablation showed that the FDA-to-SDA step produced consistent but moderate improvements, whereas the SDA-to-SDA-SCA step provided larger and more stable gains. These results indicate that second-dimension features improve the representation of neighborhood context, and their predictive value is further strengthened when coupled with spatial stratification. SHAP analysis further confirmed the substantial contribution of second-dimension features to the integrated model. The proposed framework provides an extensible pathway for spatial prediction tasks requiring the joint representation of local attributes, neighborhood context, and spatial heterogeneity.
